segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
The fairest schedule I ever wrote lasted eleven minutes.

That was generous.

It was probably dead by minute four.

East Two finally had to come apart.

Not the whole station.

The east market branch.

The old bronze structures beneath it had moved enough that even I stopped pretending restricted operation was a long-term plan.

Tova did not say I told you so.

That was almost worse.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
District engineering built a temporary bypass that could carry about sixty percent of normal winter demand while crews opened the foundation and rebuilt the branch supports.

Sixty percent is an excellent number until one hundred percent of people want heat.

Halden called me into a planning room with Tova, Pell, two market representatives, and a city service clerk.

Forty-three buildings.

Same branch.

Same shortage.

“We rotate,” Pell said.

“Obviously,” I said.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
Tova looked at me.

“Nothing is obvious before the schedule exists.”

“Fine. We probably rotate.”

“Better.”

The clinic needed continuous baseline service.

School kitchen needed mornings.

Bakeries wanted before dawn.

Markets wanted midday wash and cooling.

Apartments wanted mornings and evenings.

The public bath wanted everything because public baths are greedy by design.

We started with equal hours.

Six groups.

Four hours each.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
Same daily service for every ordinary building.

I looked at the finished page.

“Fair.”

Tova said nothing.

Halden said nothing.

The butcher, Orr, said, “No.”

I looked at him.

“What?”

“My cold room gets heat from the exchanger.”

“Cold room gets heat.”

“Yes.”

“That sentence is upsetting.”

“Absorption unit.”

“I know how it works.”

“Then stop looking upset.”

“If you take midday, I lose the cool cycle when deliveries arrive.”

“You have evening.”

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
“I do not receive meat in the evening.”

The laundry representative pointed at Group Four.

“You put washhouses off between second and sixth bell.”

“Yes.”

“That is when we work.”

“You have six to ten.”

“That is when people collect.”

“You can change hours for nine days.”

She stared at me.

There are sentences that reveal you have never run a washhouse.

Apparently I had found one.

The schedule died.

Minute eleven at the latest.

We tried again.

Use-based windows.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
Bakeries early.

Markets midday.

Apartments morning and evening.

Laundry daytime.

Bath reduced.

Clinic continuous.

School morning.

It looked better.

Then I brought it home.

Nessa read it over dinner.

“Who did you ask?”

“Market representatives.”

“Who?”

I told her.

“Apartment tenants?”

“Building owners have the notice.”

“That wasn't what I asked.”

“The apartment windows are morning and evening.”

“Which morning?”

“First to fourth bell.”

“And evening?”

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
“Seventh to tenth.”

“Night crews sleep when?”

I stopped.

Of course.

East Four had night crews.

So did bakeries.

Markets.

Tram.

Healers.

People who cleaned all of those places after everyone else left.

“Our fair schedule gets cold for people who sleep during the day.”

“Not gets cold.”

“Yes, yes. Accuracy.”

She kept reading.

“What about hot water?”

“Same feed.”

“So everyone cooks, washes, and heats rooms inside the same evening window.”

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
“The bypass model accounts for simultaneous use.”

“From what?”

“Building demand records.”

“How old?”

I checked.

Nine years.

Some updates.

Not all.

One apartment block had added attic rooms.

A printer occupied what used to be storage.

Mina's bakery had expanded the back ovens.

The bathhouse had added laundry.

Reality again.

Refusing four kinds of ink.

“We need current draw,” I said.

Nessa took another bite.

“Yes.”

“You could have said that first.”

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
“You were proud of your schedule.”

“That was cruel.”

“It lasted eleven minutes?”

“Approximately.”

She smiled.

The next day we stopped scheduling and started asking.

That was slower.

Halden hated it for the practical reason that repair started in twelve days.

“We cannot interview forty-three buildings.”

“Why not?”

“Twelve days.”

“Tova and I can split.”

“You have inspections.”

“Move them.”

“Private contracts.”

“Move them.”

He looked at me.

segments.speaker: greg
segments.transcript:
“You understand you are proving time is also an allocated resource.”

“Yes.”

“Good. I wanted you to hear it.”

Asshole.

We did not interview forty-three buildings.

We grouped them and asked enough people to discover where the records lied by age.

Mina needed strong bakery service from third to sixth bell, not first.

I had lived upstairs and still guessed wrong.
